name: John the Baptist

seo.title: Saint John the Baptist: his life, his words and how he died
seo.description: John the Baptist in plain words: the voice in the wilderness, baptising Jesus, how Herod had him killed, his feast days, and the myths.

band.lede: The voice in the wilderness. He baptised Jesus, pointed his own followers to Him, and was beheaded for telling a ruler the truth.

picture.alt: A painting by Jan van Eyck: John the Baptist, with long dark curling hair and a thick dark beard, sits turned a little to one side and looks out calmly. He wears a rough camel-hair garment under a green cloak fastened with a jewelled clasp, and an open book rests on his lap. Behind his head is a gold arch lettered in Latin, with thin gold rays like a halo.

who: John was a prophet, the son of an old priest named Zechariah. He lived in the wilderness and baptised crowds in the Jordan River. He called people to turn back to God. He baptised Jesus, and pointed his own followers to Him. For condemning the marriage of Herod, ruler of Galilee, he was beheaded.

tidbits.text: The names of the notes come from a hymn to him, *Ut queant laxis*. Its first six lines start on rising notes: **ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la**. The monk Guido of Arezzo used them to teach singing in the 1000s. Ut later became **do**.

cite.text: Britannica, “Solmization”; Catholic Encyclopedia, “St. John the Baptist”

tidbits.text: His feast falls at midsummer, and Christmas at midwinter. Augustine saw John's own words in that: Christ “was born when the days were just beginning to lengthen; John was born when they began to shorten.”

cite.text: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John, Tractate 14

tidbits.text: The Orthodox keep the day of his beheading as a **strict fast**. In some places people will not eat from a flat plate, use a knife, or eat anything round that day.

cite.text: OCA, The Beheading of John the Baptist

facts.label: Born
facts.text: In “a town in the hill country of Judah”, Luke says, without naming it. Tradition has placed it at **Ein Karem**, near Jerusalem, since at least 530, says *Britannica*.

facts.label: Parents
facts.text: **Zechariah**, a priest of the division of Abijah, and **Elizabeth**, a descendant of Aaron. They had long been childless, and were “both well along in years”.

facts.label: Home
facts.text: The **wilderness** of Judea, from his youth until he began to preach.

facts.label: Work
facts.text: A **prophet** and **baptiser**. He preached and baptised along the Jordan, at **Bethany beyond the Jordan** and at **Aenon near Salim**.

facts.label: Dress and food
facts.text: A garment of **camel's hair** with a **leather belt**. He lived on **locusts and wild honey**, and never drank wine.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **John the Baptizer**, which is what “the Baptist” means. **The Forerunner**, in the Orthodox Church. **The Precursor**, in older Catholic writing.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: Beheaded in prison on the order of **Herod Antipas**, ruler of Galilee, some time between 28 and 36. Josephus names the place: the fortress of **Machaerus**, on Herod's border with the king of Arabia.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: His disciples laid his body in a tomb. His tomb has been shown at **Sebaste**, in Samaria, since about 360, says *Britannica*.

portrait.alt: A Russian icon on a gold ground: John the Baptist, with long hair and a beard, stands on a rocky hill with great brown wings spread behind him. He wears a camel-hair tunic under a dark green cloak and holds an unrolled scroll. With one hand he points to a bowl in which the Christ Child lies. Above him, a small blessing figure appears in the clouds.
portrait.credit: Saint John the Forerunner, a Russian icon of the 1800s. Chester Beatty Library, Dublin. Public domain.
portrait.caption: A Russian icon of the 1800s, now in Dublin. Some icons give him wings: Jesus called him God's “messenger”, and in Greek the word is *angelos*. He points to the Christ Child in a bowl. Public domain.

typeNote: The test names him for his steadiness. He lived in the wilderness until the day he began to preach. Jesus asked if the crowds had gone out to see “a reed swaying in the wind”, and Gregory the Great says a reed bends to praise or blame, but “no variety of circumstance bent him from his uprightness”.

west.text: His **birth**, a **Catholic** solemnity. A Festival in the **Church of England**. Also the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.
His **beheading**. For **Catholics** it is the Passion of Saint John the Baptist, a memorial. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church** and the **Missouri Synod**.

east.text: The **Synaxis** of John, the day after Theophany, the feast of Jesus' baptism. **OCA**.
The **first and second finding** of his head. **OCA**.
The **third finding** of his head, about 850. **OCA**.
The **Coptic** Church keeps his birth on 30 Paoni, which falls on this day.
The **Coptic** Church keeps his martyrdom on 2 Tout: 12 September, or 13 September in the year before a leap year.

feasts.note: Why 24 June? Luke says Elizabeth was six months pregnant when Gabriel came to Mary, so John's birth is kept six months before Christmas. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* calls it perhaps the oldest feast of any saint. Rome's 1916 book of martyrs says he was killed “about the feast of Easter”. It keeps 29 August as the day his head “was found for the second time”. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later: his birth on 7 July, his beheading on 11 September.

moments.title: An angel at the altar
moments.text: His parents, Zechariah and Elizabeth, were righteous, old and childless. Zechariah was a priest. One day he was chosen by lot to burn incense in the temple. An angel appeared beside the altar. “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to give him the name John.” Zechariah asked, “How can I be sure of this?” The angel answered, “I am Gabriel.” Because Zechariah did not believe, he would be silent until it came to pass. He came out unable to speak, and could only make signs to the people.

moments.title: The leap in the womb
moments.text: In Elizabeth's sixth month, Gabriel was sent to Mary at Nazareth. He told her that her relative Elizabeth was expecting a son. Mary hurried to the hill country to see her. When Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting, the baby leaped in her womb. Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and cried out, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!” Why should “the mother of my Lord” come to her? “As soon as the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the baby in my womb leaped for joy.” Mary stayed with her about three months.

moments.title: “His name is John”
moments.text: Elizabeth gave birth to a son, and her neighbours rejoiced with her. On the eighth day they were going to name him Zechariah, after his father. His mother said no: “He shall be called John.” “There is no one among your relatives who bears this name.” So they made signs to his father. Zechariah asked for a tablet and wrote, “His name is John.” At once he could speak again, and he began to praise God. People all over the hill country asked, “What then will this child become?”

moments.title: The voice in the wilderness
moments.text: John grew up in the wilderness. Then, in the fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius, “the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness.” He went all through the Jordan valley, preaching a baptism of repentance. Isaiah had written of him: “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord.’” He wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt. His food was locusts and wild honey. People went out to him from Jerusalem and all Judea. Confessing their sins, they were baptised by him in the Jordan.

moments.title: “What then should we do?”
moments.text: John did not flatter the crowds who came out to him. “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” he asked. “Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance.” The crowds asked him, “What then should we do?” He told them to share their food and their clothes. Even tax collectors came. “Collect no more than you are authorized,” he said. The people began to wonder if John might be the Christ. He told them that One more powerful was coming, “the straps of Whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.”

moments.title: The baptism of Jesus
moments.text: Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptised by John. John tried to stop Him. “I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?” “Let it be so now,” Jesus replied. “It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness in this way.” So John baptised Him. As Jesus came up out of the water, the heavens opened. John later told what he saw: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him.” And a voice from heaven said, “This is My beloved Son, in Whom I am well pleased!”

moments.title: “Who are you?”
moments.text: The leaders in Jerusalem sent priests and Levites to ask John who he was. He did not dodge the question: “I am not the Christ.” “Are you Elijah?” “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” “No.” At last they asked, “What do you say about yourself?” He answered in the words of Isaiah: “I am a voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way for the Lord.’” Jesus would say something else about Elijah: see Was he Elijah?, below.

moments.title: “Look, the Lamb of God!”
moments.text: The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him. “Look, the Lamb of God, Who takes away the sin of the world!” The day after, he was standing with two of his own disciples. As Jesus walked by, John said it again: “Look, the Lamb of God!” The two left John and followed Jesus. One of them was Andrew. He went and found his brother Simon: “We have found the Messiah.”

moments.title: Arrested
moments.text: Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee, had married Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip. John kept telling him, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife!” So Herod had him arrested, bound and put in prison. Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted him dead. But Herod feared John, “knowing that he was a righteous and holy man.” When he heard John speak, he was greatly perplexed, “yet he listened to him gladly.”

moments.title: A question from prison
moments.text: In prison, John heard about the works of Christ. He sent two of his disciples to ask Him, “Are You the One Who was to come, or should we look for someone else?” Jesus sent them back with an answer: “The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor.” As they left, He turned to the crowds. “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind?” Did John doubt? Hilary, Jerome and Chrysostom all say no. He asked for his disciples' sake, so that they would see for themselves.

cite.text: Matthew 11:2-11; Luke 7:18-28; Hilary, Jerome and Chrysostom, in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 11

words.note: John wrote nothing. The four Gospels record his words. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

feature.kicker: When the crowds went to Jesus
feature.q: He must increase; I must decrease.
feature.ctx: John was still baptising at Aenon, where the water was plentiful. His disciples came to him upset: “He is baptizing, and everyone is going to Him.” John answered that he was only the friend of the bridegroom. “That joy is mine, and it is now complete.”

extras.title: Was he Elijah?
extras.lede: The book of Malachi ends with a promise: “I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD” (Malachi 4:5). Was John that Elijah? The Gospels seem to answer both ways. Here each answer speaks in its own words.

items.title: Yes, said Jesus
items.text: Jesus told the crowds that John was the one Malachi promised. After the Transfiguration He said it again, that Elijah had already come and was not recognised. Then “the disciples understood that He was speaking to them about John the Baptist.”
items.quote: And if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come.

items.title: No, said John
items.text: When the priests and Levites asked him, “Are you Elijah?”, he would not take the title. He called himself only “a voice of one calling in the wilderness”.

items.title: In the spirit of Elijah
items.text: Before John was born, Gabriel said he would go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah”. Jerome read Jesus' words that way. John is called Elijah, he says, not because a soul passed into a new body, as some taught, but because he came in Elijah's spirit and power. And the two lives rhymed. Both lived in the wilderness, and both wore a leather belt. The old translation spells Elijah as Elias:
items.quote: because he reproved Ahab and Jezebel for their wickedness, Elias was compelled to fly; because he condemned the unlawful union of Herod and Herodias, John is beheaded.

cite.text: Luke 1:17; 2 Kings 1:8; Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 11, tr. 1841

items.title: Two forerunners
items.text: John Chrysostom read Malachi's two promises as one: God's messenger who prepares the way, and Elijah the prophet. Each was to come before the Lord. So he could say the names round both ways:
items.quote: John the Baptist is Elias, and Elias is John, because both were forerunners of Christ.

cite.text: Malachi 3:1 and 4:5; John Chrysostom, in the Catena Aurea on Matthew 11, tr. 1841

myths.truth: The Gospels say his food was “locusts and wild honey”. The law of Moses allowed locusts as food: “you may eat any kind of locust, katydid, cricket, or grasshopper.” The carob idea is a belief, not what the text says. It gave the carob tree two English names, **locust bean** and **St John's bread**, says *Britannica*.

myths.claim: The dancer was Salome, and she danced the dance of the seven veils.
myths.truth: The Gospels never name her. They call her “the daughter of Herodias”. The name comes from Josephus, who says Herodias had a daughter named Salome, later married to Philip the tetrarch. He says nothing of a dance. The seven veils come from Oscar Wilde's play *Salomé*, written in French in 1892. Its stage direction reads, “Salomé dances the dance of the seven veils.”

cite.text: Mark 6:22; Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapter 5; Oscar Wilde, Salomé, tr. Alfred Douglas (1894)

myths.claim: John the Baptist was a Baptist.
myths.truth: “Baptist” was his title, not his church. It means the one who baptises, and Josephus already calls him “John, that was called the Baptist”. The Baptist churches came some 1,600 years later. Most scholars, says *Britannica*, trace them to 17th-century Puritanism. They hold that only believers should be baptised, by immersion.

cite.text: Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapter 5; Catholic Encyclopedia; Britannica, “Baptist”

myths.claim: The Herod who killed John also killed the babies of Bethlehem.
myths.truth: They were father and son. King Herod, called the Great, died while Jesus was still a child. The Herod who killed John was his son, Herod Antipas, “Herod the tetrarch”, ruler of Galilee. He was the Herod to whom Pilate later sent Jesus. He questioned Jesus at length, then mocked Him and sent Him back.

cite.text: Matthew 2:19-22; 14:1-12; Luke 23:6-12; Josephus, Antiquities, book 18, chapter 5

circle.name: Zechariah
circle.text: His father, a priest. He doubted the angel and was struck silent until John was named. Then he sang the song the Church calls the **Benedictus**.

circle.name: Elizabeth
circle.text: His mother, a descendant of Aaron. Long childless, she kept to herself for five months and said, “The Lord has done this for me.”

circle.name: Mary
circle.text: Elizabeth's relative. Luke never says how they were related, so John and Jesus were kin, but not certainly cousins. When Mary came to visit, the unborn John leaped for joy. She stayed about three months.

circle.name: Jesus
circle.text: John baptised Him in the Jordan and pointed his own disciples to Him. Jesus said no one born of women was greater than John. When He heard John had been killed, He withdrew by boat to a solitary place.

circle.name: Andrew
circle.text: One of John's disciples. He heard John call Jesus the Lamb of God, followed Jesus, and brought his brother Simon Peter.

circle.name: His disciples
circle.text: They fasted often, and John taught them to pray. After his death they took his body, buried it, and went and told Jesus.

circle.name: Herod Antipas
circle.text: Ruler of Galilee. He jailed John for condemning his marriage, yet liked to listen to him. He had him beheaded rather than break an oath made before his guests.

circle.name: Herodias
circle.text: Herod's wife, who had been his brother Philip's wife. She held a grudge against John and told her daughter to ask for his head.

circle.name: The daughter of Herodias
circle.text: She danced at Herod's birthday banquet, and asked for John's head at her mother's word. The Gospels do not name her. Josephus names Herodias's daughter as Salome.

death.big: Herod Antipas had him beheaded in prison, at the wish of Herodias. Josephus says it was at the fortress of Machaerus.
paras: On his birthday, Herod gave a banquet for his nobles and commanders and the leading men of Galilee. The daughter of Herodias danced, and pleased Herod and his guests. He swore to give her whatever she asked, “up to half my kingdom!” She went out and asked her mother, “What should I request?” Herodias answered, “The head of John the Baptist.” The king was consumed with sorrow. But because of his oaths and his guests, he did not want to refuse her. He sent an executioner, who beheaded John in the prison.
When John's disciples heard, they came and took his body and laid it in a tomb. Then they went and told Jesus. When Jesus heard about John, “He withdrew by boat privately to a solitary place.”
Afterwards, when Herod heard what Jesus was doing, he was sure he knew who it was: “John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead!”

The Jewish historian Josephus tells it without the dance. Herod feared “lest the great influence John had over the people might put it into his power and inclination to raise a rebellion”. So John was sent in chains to Machaerus, “and was there put to death.” Later, Herod's army was destroyed in a war with Aretas, king of Arabia. Some of the Jews thought that “came from God, and that very justly, as a punishment of what he did against John”.
His tomb was later shown at Sebaste, in Samaria. Theodoret says that under the emperor Julian, pagans opened it: “his bones burnt, and the ashes scattered abroad.”

later.title: Where is his head?
later.text: Several churches have claimed it. The Orthodox tell of three findings: on the Mount of Olives, near Emesa in 452, and a third about 850. The Coptic synaxarium says it is “present at Homs in Syria”, which is Emesa. Rome's 1916 book of martyrs says it was carried to Rome, to the church of St Silvester. Amiens in France claims it too. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* admits the many accounts are “so intricate as to baffle solution”.

cite.text: OCA, 24 February and 25 May; Coptic Synaxarium, 2 Tout; The Roman Martyrology (1916), 29 August; Catholic Encyclopedia, “St. John the Baptist”

saint.big: Yes. Every church that keeps saints' days honours him, and his birth is kept as a feast, as only Christ's and Mary's are besides.

paras: Is he an Old Testament saint or a New Testament one? He stands on the line between them. Jesus said, “all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John.”
The Orthodox call him the Forerunner, {el|Prodromos}: the one who runs ahead. The OCA puts his place like this:

quotes.q: Saint John, the holy Forerunner and Baptist of the Lord, whom the Lord called the greatest of the prophets, concludes the history of the Old Testament and opens the era of the New Testament.

cite.text: OCA, Synaxis of the Holy Glorious Prophet, Forerunner and Baptist John
